title: Planning with HTN and Evolutionary Search
service: HTNPlan: a ChatHTN-style HTN planner with a scripted LLM fallback and learned decompositions, an INI method library, an AlphaEvolve-style evolutionary search with a deterministic evaluator, an async mutation ensemble reported as CSV, and decomposition trees with an independent replay check

parts.lesson_anchor: Hierarchical Task Networks; ChatHTN steps 1-5 (validate against the operator schema, reject invalid decompositions; the symbolic layer owns correctness); Online method learning; Where this pattern goes wrong: HTN without operators; code/main.py HTNPlanner.plan and _expand; Exercise 1 (backtracking); quiz Q9 and Q10 (cache before verify, try every method, then the cache, then the LLM); skill file: cache successful LLM decompositions
planted_bugs: _plan tries only applicable[0] and asks the LLM only when no method's preconditions hold: release comes back None with no exception, two decompositions above the real choice, where deploy_canary's watch_canary fails and deploy_direct is never tried

an LLM reply is written into cached_methods before it expands (the lesson code's order): ('open_pr',) is learned although it fails from {'logged_in'}; without the direct check the poisoned entry shows up one request later
a learned decomposition that fails from a new state returns None without falling back to the LLM
with backtracking, a (task, state) that failed is searched again on every path: a dead end behind 18 two-way waves costs 2^18 paths and 524,287 LLM calls
parts.timing_assert: plan('rollout') behind an 18-wave dead end under 0.05 s: without the failure record 0.70-0.74 s on this machine (load average about 4.5), with it about 50 microseconds and 19 LLM calls
parts.overfix_guard: the failure record is keyed by the state as well as the task (redeploy: deploy fails before the build and must work after it) and lives for one plan() call only (hotfix is asked again on the next request, so a record kept on the instance or an LLM-reply cache fails); replies naming anything outside the schema are rejected whole before expansion (trimming the unknown name learns ('open_editor',)); a reply that fails leaves the learned decomposition in place (writing it to the cache first and deleting it on failure loses SHIP); methods keep library order (fewest-subtasks-first picks direct over canary); library before learned before LLM; an expansion cap stops the dead end but still costs 4999 LLM calls; the caller's state is never changed

clarifying_questions: which of several problems to report

deviations: Part 1: the lesson's plan(task, state, depth, max_depth) becomes plan(task, state) with max_depth a planner field, because the lesson's _expand does not pass max_depth down and a per-call failure record needs a clear start of the call. Following quiz Q10, the LLM is the fallback whenever no library method and no learned decomposition expands, not only when no method's preconditions hold; the starter keeps the lesson's narrower condition as part of the first bug. The docstring states the per-call rule (a task that failed from a state is not tried from it again), so the LLM-call count in the timing block is a documented contract. The scripted LLM gives out a list of replies per task in order, so that asking again can give a different answer.
Part 1: the failure record is keyed by (task, state) without the depth, as the docstring says; the depth caveat is an interviewer follow-up rather than a test.

Part 2: the default optionxform is not a trap here. With one section per method every key is a fixed lowercase field name, and section names keep their case in configparser. The whitespace trap comes from a free-text note per method instead, which also brings in the comment-line and trailing-newline losses of multi-line values.

Part 3: genomes are the lesson's own (a, b) coefficients of a x + b with its target 3x + 7 and its random_mutation, so the search is lesson-grown rather than a new program representation. Every mutation draws from random.Random(f'{seed}/{generation}/{parent}/{mutator}'), fixed by its place in the run, instead of one shared generator: that is what makes Part 4's concurrent ensemble reproducible, and it replaces the lesson's global random.seed. The target is checked at generation ends, the budget immediately.

Part 4: there is no evaluator lock. The evaluator scores children one at a time in evolve()'s slot order, each as soon as it and the ones before it are ready; a lock with completion-order evaluation would make a mid-generation budget cut depend on timing. The test compares the CSV rows with evolve() for the same arguments under two latency orders, and adds a model that never answers to test cancellation.

Part 5: the planner's tree is built by the same search as plan() (the reference's _plan returns nodes, and plan() reads the leaves), so Part 5 refactors the Part 1 planner. The check also enforces the method structure (children equal the method's subtasks, the method belongs to the node's task), not only operator preconditions, because a primitive sequence that runs is not by itself a valid HTN decomposition.
